newsitem.title: USA: Trans-World determined to safeguard activities.
newsitem.headline: Trans-World determined to safeguard activities.

text.p: Bruised after being booted out of Russia's Krasnoyarsk smelter back in October 1994, the $6 billion sales a year Trans-World Group is determined to protect minority shareholdings in two other aluminum plants from protectionist overtures of politicians.
Trans-World Group which has cornered a third of Russia's huge aluminum output, has just launched a global media blitz led by a battery of lawyers to safeguard its money-spinning smelting activities.

The latest move was a full-page advertisement in Friday's edition of the International Herald Tribune newspaper carrying an open letter to U.S. Vice President Al Gore and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin saying foreign investment in Russia was in peril.
The privately-owned company's share are equally held by two brothers, David and Simon Reuben. The former's involvement in Russian metals dates back to the late 1960s.

The brothers told reporters of "orchestrated campaigns" against them, anti-semitism, attempted blackmail, KGB complicity with detractors to keep Trans-World out of Russia, and shifting power alliances in Russian politics.

Using what clout it has to clear its name, Trans-World met British Foreign Office officials last week, will talk to U.S. State Department representatives on Monday, and requested an interview with Chernomyrdin.
Allegations against Trans-World have been swirling around in the turbulent world of Russian aluminum for some time.
"We are extremely legal and extremely above board," David Reuben, Trans-World's executive chairman, said.
Clearing the company's name was vital to avoid being shunned by Western companies, the company's lawyers said.

The three key allegations Trans-World is refuting are that it defrauded the Russian Central Bank, that the deaths of three bankers were linked to the company's efforts to wrestle back a 29 percent stake in Krasnoyarsk, and that it had been supporting the Russian politician Oleg Soskovets, seen close to would-be president, Alexander Lebed.

Trans-World's anxieties came to a head on February 21 when Russian Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov told the Duma parliament that domestic aluminum producers should be protected from Western companies.
Imports of raw materials to make aluminum should also be slapped with duties, Kulikov suggested.
The minister named a Trans-World associate, Trans-CIS Commodities, as allegedly dealing in fraudulent contracts with Russian smelters such as Krasnoyarsk.
David Reuben said Trans-CIS and its head, Lev Tchernoi were exonerated of all allegations by the Russian Interior Ministry.
But Kulikov's remarks have been echoed by others in the Russian aluminum industry who choke at the thought of foreign tolling companies creaming hard currency profits from domestic assets.
Trans-World is a leading supplier of alumina to Russia for tolling into metal.
The company is also fighting in Moscow's federal courts to have reinstated its 29 percent stake in Krasnoyarsk which was delisted by the smelter's management.
"I think the court in Moscow will come down on our side. If it comes down on the opposite side then every investment is a risk," Simon Reuben, vice-chairman of Trans-World Group said.

Trans-World said it has some $1 billion in assets in Russia where it employs 130,000 people. The company stresses it is just a minority partner in the smelters, but privately agreed that without Trans-World supplying cash up front to buy alumina, power and transport, the smelters would probably have closed.

But despite Kulikov's talk of protecting the Russian aluminum industry from criminals in the interests of national security, Reuben conceded that confiscation of its shares in smelters by the government appeared unlikely because the country lacked cash.
"I am not concerned about outright takeover, but I am concerned they talk about putting on import duties. When you start doing that then the U.S. will reciprocate," Reuben said.

Trans-World has heard nothing from Russian government officials since Kulikov gave his speech, but this did not stop Reuben from saying Wednesday that $500 million will be ploughed into Bratsk and Sayansk to increase production over the coming years.
